title: Who pays a sugar tax?
text:
← PUBADM 513

Suppose Boise puts a tax on sugary drinks, collected from sellers. Who ends up paying it: the people buying soda, or the stores selling it? How much money does it raise, and how much buying and selling simply stops happening? Move the sliders and find out. This is the model behind Doing Economics Lab 2, which uses data from Berkeley’s real soda tax.


viewof t = Inputs.range([0, 1], {step: 0.05, value: 0.5, label: "Tax ($ per liter)"})
viewof buyerResp = Inputs.range([1, 5], {step: 0.5, value: 2, label: "How much buyers cut back (1–5)"})
viewof sellerResp = Inputs.range([1, 5], {step: 0.5, value: 2, label: "How much sellers cut back (1–5)"})























Q0 = 100
P0 = 2
b = 0.04 / buyerResp
d = 0.02 / sellerResp
a = P0 + b * Q0
c = P0 - d * Q0
Qt = Math.max(0, Q0 - t / (b + d))
Pb = a - b * Qt
Ps = Pb - t
buyerShare = t > 0 ? (Pb - P0) / t : d / (b + d)
revenue = t * Qt
dwl = 0.5 * t * (Q0 - Qt)
cs = 0.5 * (a - Pb) * Qt
ps = 0.5 * (Ps - c) * Qt
band = (from, to, lo, hi) => d3.range(from, to + 1e-9, Math.max((to - from) / 60, 1e-6)).map(q => ({q, lo: lo(q), hi: hi(q)}))
curve = f => d3.range(0, 201, 2).map(q => ({q, p: f(q)}))



















































































































Plot.plot({
  width: 820,
  height: 470,
  marginLeft: 56,
  marginBottom: 46,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {domain: [0, 200], label: "Soda sold (thousand liters per week) →"},
  y: {domain: [0, 6], label: "↑ Price ($ per liter)", grid: true},
  clip: true,
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(band(0, Qt, () => Pb, q => a - b * q), {x: "q", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: "#176b87", fillOpacity: 0.22}),
    Plot.areaY(band(0, Qt, q => c + d * q, () => Ps), {x: "q", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: "#e5ad3d", fillOpacity: 0.3}),
    Plot.areaY(band(0, Qt, () => Ps, () => Pb), {x: "q", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: "#2f7d5b", fillOpacity: 0.3}),
    Plot.areaY(band(Qt, Q0, q => c + d * q, q => a - b * q), {x: "q", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: "#c24f3d", fillOpacity: 0.45}),
    Plot.line(curve(q => a - b * q), {x: "q", y: "p", stroke: "#176b87", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line(curve(q => c + d * q), {x: "q", y: "p", stroke: "#b07d12", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line(curve(q => c + d * q + t), {x: "q", y: "p", stroke: "#b07d12", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6 5"}),
    Plot.ruleY([Pb, Ps], {x1: 0, x2: Qt, stroke: "#102a43", strokeDasharray: "2 4"}),
    Plot.ruleX([Qt], {y1: 0, y2: Pb, stroke: "#102a43", strokeDasharray: "2 4"}),
    Plot.dot([{q: Q0, p: P0}], {x: "q", y: "p", r: 5, fill: "#fff", stroke: "#102a43", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot([{q: Qt, p: Pb}, {q: Qt, p: Ps}], {x: "q", y: "p", r: 5, fill: "#102a43"}),
    Plot.text([{q: 196, p: a - b * 196}], {x: "q", y: "p", text: () => "Demand", dy: -12, textAnchor: "end", fill: "#176b87", fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.text([{q: 196, p: Math.min(5.8, c + d * 196)}], {x: "q", y: "p", text: () => "Supply", dy: 14, textAnchor: "end", fill: "#b07d12", fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.text([{q: 196, p: Math.min(5.8, c + d * 196 + t)}], {x: "q", y: "p", text: () => t > 0 ? "Supply + tax" : "", dy: -10, textAnchor: "end", fill: "#b07d12"}),
    Plot.text([{q: Q0, p: P0}], {x: "q", y: "p", text: () => "No-tax equilibrium", dx: 10, dy: 16, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#597287"})
  ]
})







swatch = (color, opacity, label) => html`<span style="display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:.4rem;margin-right:1.1rem"><span style="width:14px;height:14px;background:${color};opacity:${opacity}"></span>${label}</span>`
html`<div style="font-size:.9rem;color:#597287">
${swatch("#176b87", .5, "Buyers' gain (consumer surplus)")}
${swatch("#e5ad3d", .6, "Sellers' gain (producer surplus)")}
${swatch("#2f7d5b", .6, "Tax revenue")}
${swatch("#c24f3d", .7, "Deadweight loss")}
</div>`

















money = x => "$" + d3.format(",.0f")(x * 1000)
html`<div class="stat-row">
  <div class="stat"><div class="k">Price buyers pay</div><div class="v">$${Pb.toFixed(2)}</div></div>
  <div class="stat"><div class="k">Price sellers keep</div><div class="v">$${Ps.toFixed(2)}</div></div>
  <div class="stat"><div class="k">Share paid by buyers</div><div class="v">${Math.round(100 * buyerShare)}%</div></div>
  <div class="stat"><div class="k">Soda sold</div><div class="v">${Qt.toFixed(0)}k L <span style="font-size:.85rem;color:#597287">(${Qt < Q0 ? "−" + (100 * (Q0 - Qt) / Q0).toFixed(0) + "%" : "no change"})</span></div></div>
  <div class="stat"><div class="k">Tax revenue / week</div><div class="v">${money(revenue)}</div></div>
  <div class="stat" style="border-left-color:#c24f3d"><div class="k">Deadweight loss / week</div><div class="v">${money(dwl)}</div></div>
</div>`
















Try this

Set buyers’ response to 1: people keep buying soda almost no matter the price. Who pays most of the tax now? What happens to the deadweight loss?
Now set buyers’ response to 5. The tax shifts toward sellers, sales fall more, and revenue drops. If the goal is public health rather than revenue, which world do you want to be in?
Double the tax from $0.50 to $1.00. Does the deadweight loss double, or do something else? Why?
The statute says sellers pay the tax. Does that decide who actually pays it?


Read more: ESPP Unit 7, Firms and markets for goods and services and 3.13 Doing Economics: Measuring the effect of a sugar tax.

Economics is easier to understand once you’ve been part of it. Each week we start by being the economic actors ourselves. Then we draw the model that explains what happened, and use it on a real policy question.




Step 1



A short live experiment, run on your phone or with a deck of cards. We contribute to a public good, make and reject offers, trade in a market, and bargain over wages.




Step 2



We build the textbook model from our own results, using interactive figures where you move the sliders and watch what changes.




Step 3



We apply the model to a live policy, often an Idaho one. All semester you’ll work as the economist on one policy you choose.







These are interactive figures for the graphs that matter most. Change the inputs and see what the model predicts.




Units 3 & 7



Supply, demand, and a per-unit tax. See how the tax splits between buyers and sellers, what it raises, and what it costs in lost trades.




Unit 5



Compare Idaho and the US using Census data, then build your own economy and watch the Gini change.







Read the unit after class, once you’ve seen the model in action. Each lab night we do a Doing Economics project together in Excel.

title: Lorenz curves and the Gini coefficient
text:
← PUBADM 513

Line up every household from poorest to richest. A Lorenz curve asks: what share of all income goes to the bottom 20%? The bottom 40%? If income were shared equally, the curve would follow the diagonal. The Gini coefficient measures the gap between the diagonal and the curve. It runs from 0 (everyone has the same income) to 1 (one household has everything).


census = ({
  "Idaho": {shares: [3.89, 9.90, 15.70, 23.04, 47.48], gini: 0.4345},
  "United States": {shares: [3.00, 8.55, 14.39, 22.59, 51.47], gini: 0.4809}
})
lorenz = shares => {
  const total = d3.sum(shares)
  let cum = 0
  return [{x: 0, y: 0}, ...shares.map((s, i) => ({x: (i + 1) / 5, y: (cum += s / total)}))]
}
// Trapezoid rule on five quintile points
giniOf = pts => 1 - d3.sum(pts.slice(1), (p, i) => (p.x - pts[i].x) * (p.y + pts[i].y))
























viewof place = Inputs.radio(["Idaho", "United States"], {value: "Idaho", label: "Compare with"})






Build your own economy. Here is the average household income in each fifth, in thousands of dollars:

viewof q1 = Inputs.range([0, 400], {step: 5, value: 15, label: "Poorest 20%"})
viewof q2 = Inputs.range([0, 400], {step: 5, value: 40, label: "Next 20%"})
viewof q3 = Inputs.range([0, 400], {step: 5, value: 65, label: "Middle 20%"})
viewof q4 = Inputs.range([0, 400], {step: 5, value: 100, label: "Next 20%"})
viewof q5 = Inputs.range([0, 400], {step: 5, value: 230, label: "Richest 20%"})





































mine = lorenz([q1, q2, q3, q4, q5])
theirs = lorenz(census[place].shares)
myGini = d3.sum([q1, q2, q3, q4, q5]) > 0 ? giniOf(mine) : NaN
theirGini = giniOf(theirs)
Plot.plot({
  width: 560,
  height: 520,
  marginLeft: 56,
  marginBottom: 46,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Share of households, poorest to richest →", tickFormat: "%"},
  y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "↑ Share of all income", tickFormat: "%", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(theirs, {x: "x", y1: "y", y2: "x", fill: "#176b87", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.line([{x: 0, y: 0}, {x: 1, y: 1}], {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#597287", strokeDasharray: "5 5"}),
    Plot.line(theirs, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#176b87", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.dot(theirs, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "#176b87", r: 4}),
    Plot.line(mine, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#2f7d5b", strokeWidth: 3, strokeDasharray: "8 4"}),
    Plot.dot(mine, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "#2f7d5b", r: 4}),
    Plot.text([{x: 0.55, y: 0.6}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => "Perfect equality", rotate: -45, fill: "#597287", dy: -8}),
    Plot.text([{x: 0.8, y: theirs[4].y}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => place, dx: 8, dy: 14, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#176b87", fontWeight: 700}),
    Plot.text([{x: 0.6, y: mine[3].y}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => "Your economy", dx: 8, dy: 14, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#2f7d5b", fontWeight: 700})
  ]
})






































html`<div class="stat-row">
  <div class="stat" style="border-left-color:#2f7d5b"><div class="k">Your economy · Gini</div><div class="v">${isNaN(myGini) ? "—" : myGini.toFixed(3)}</div></div>
  <div class="stat"><div class="k">${place} · Gini from these 5 points</div><div class="v">${theirGini.toFixed(3)}</div></div>
  <div class="stat"><div class="k">${place} · official Census Gini</div><div class="v">${census[place].gini.toFixed(3)}</div></div>
  <div class="stat" style="border-left-color:#e5ad3d"><div class="k">Richest 20% / poorest 20% (yours)</div><div class="v">${q1 > 0 ? (q5 / q1).toFixed(1) + "×" : "—"}</div></div>
</div>`







Try this

Set all five sliders to the same income. What does the curve look like, and what is the Gini?
Now double every household’s income. Does the Gini change? What does that tell you about what the Gini measures, and what it doesn’t?
Take $20k from the richest fifth and give it to the poorest fifth. How far does the Gini fall? Now move $20k from the middle fifth to the next fifth. Which transfer matters more?
Try to match Idaho’s curve. Then try to match the United States. What separates the two?
Why is the official Census Gini higher than the one computed from just five points? (Hint: what’s hidden inside each fifth?)


Data: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 1-year estimates, tables B19082 and B19083. Margins of error on the Gini (90% confidence): Idaho ±0.007, United States ±0.001.
Read more: ESPP 5.10, Comparing inequality across the world and 5.12 Doing Economics: Measuring inequality.
